findings.issue_text: [BUG] OptimizedCursorPaginator subclasses `BasePaginator`, a class that does not exist in sentry/api/paginator.py (the real base classes are `Paginator` and `CursorPaginator`), so the class definition raises NameError at module import. Importing sentry.api.paginator fails with `NameError: name 'BasePaginator' is not defined`, taking down every API endpoint that imports the paginator module, not just audit logs.

[BUG] The endpoint references `organization_context`, a variable that does not exist anywhere in OrganizationAuditLogsEndpoint.get(), which resolves the org via `self.get_organization(request, organization_id)`. Every GET to the audit logs endpoint raises NameError ('organization_context' is not defined) before any pagination logic runs, returning a 500 for all users including superusers.

[BUG] OptimizedCursorPaginator.get_item_key calls `int(math.floor(value))` on `getattr(item, self.key)`, but the endpoint passes `order_by="-datetime"`, so `value` is a datetime object and `math.floor(datetime)` raises TypeError. The first optimized-pagination request that returns results crashes with `TypeError: an argument is required / type datetime not convertible to float` — the real CursorPaginator avoids this via a datetime_to_int conversion that this class omits.

[BUG] The 'advanced feature' slices the queryset with a negative start (`queryset[cursor.offset:stop]` for negative offsets), which Django's ORM forbids — QuerySet slicing raises AssertionError for negative indices. Any request carrying a negative cursor offset (the exact case enable_advanced_features is designed to handle) fails with Django's `AssertionError: Negative indexing is not supported.` producing a 500; the advertised negative-offset capability cannot work against a QuerySet.

[BUG] The gate calls `organization_context.member.has_global_access`, but OrganizationMember has no `has_global_access` attribute/method (global access is exposed via member flags, e.g. `member.flags.has_global_access`). Even once organization_context is fixed, the check raises AttributeError at request time, so the optimized path can never be reached.

[ADVISORY] The diff edits the shared base Paginator.get_result to allow negative offsets when cursor.is_prev, changing behavior of every endpoint using Paginator/DateTimePaginator, not just audit logs. Existing prev-cursor pagination on all paginated endpoints silently takes the `offset` (possibly negative) branch; any caller that produces negative offsets now hits a crashing negative slice instead of the previous clamped behavior — an unreviewed cross-endpoint regression hidden inside an audit-log PR.

[BUG] The 'advanced' negative-offset branch slices the queryset with a negative start (queryset[start_offset:stop] where start_offset = cursor.offset < 0), which Django forbids, so any admin client sending a cursor with a negative offset gets a 500 (AssertionError: 'Negative indexing is not supported') instead of paginated results. The exact feature this PR advertises — negative-offset 'bidirectional pagination' — crashes on first use; the inline comment claiming 'Django ORM properly handles negative slicing automatically' is false, and the behavior is unreachable/crashing rather than optimized.

[BUG] In the modified DateTimePaginator.get_result, the is_prev branch still passes the raw cursor offset to the slice (start_offset = offset when cursor.is_prev), so a crafted prev cursor with a negative offset reaches queryset[start_offset:stop] and raises Django's AssertionError ('Negative indexing is not supported'), returning a 500. A client-controlled base64 cursor value can crash the audit-logs (and every other DateTimePaginator) endpoint; the new max(0, offset) clamp fixes only the non-prev direction, leaving the sibling case unhandled in the very hunk that touches this code.

[ADVISORY] The new OptimizedCursorPaginator duplicates CursorPaginator.get_result near-verbatim (offset/extra logic, prev trimming, build_cursor call) with no test coverage anywhere in the diff, creating a second hand-maintained copy of pagination core logic that will silently drift from the original. Any future fix to cursor pagination semantics (boundary trimming, hits caps, prev reversal) must be applied in two places; a fix applied only to CursorPaginator leaves audit logs paginating with subtly different semantics, and there are zero tests in the diff to catch it.

[ADVISORY] The optimized path is gated on a raw query parameter ('optimized_pagination' == 'true') plus an ad-hoc is_superuser/has_global_access check rather than a feature flag or endpoint option, so it cannot be disabled fleet-wide without a code deploy and is invisible to the permission system. If the negative-offset path (or any future 'advanced feature' behind this flag) misbehaves in production, operators must ship a revert; additionally the privilege check lives outside any shared permission class so it bypasses audit of how elevated pagination is granted.

[ADVISORY] organization_context.member.has_global_access will raise AttributeError (NoneType has no attribute has_global_access) whenever the requesting user has no organization member record and is not a superuser, turning an intended fallback into a 500. Any request reaching this handler from a non-member context (e.g. superuser short-circuits skipped because of 'or' ordering is fine, but non-member authenticated users that pass the endpoint's permission layer via org-context edge cases) crashes with a 500 instead of falling back to the standard paginator.

[ADVISORY] The negative-offset branch performs no validation or clamping of how far back the negative offset goes, so even if the negative-slice crash were fixed, an unbounded negative offset would be a client-controlled slice on a permission-sensitive queryset whose only stated guarantee is the comment 'permissions are checked at the queryset level'. Staff-level reviewers on the next change inherit an unvalidated, client-influenced offset bound into a security-sensitive code path with only a comment as its safety argument; the next refactor of build_queryset can silently break that assumption.

[ADVISORY] The diff adds a second pagination mode to the audit-logs endpoint (including a superuser-only branch and a new paginator class) with no test in the diff exercising either branch — no spec/test files are present in this change (verified: no test-shaped files in the diff). The gating logic (use_optimized && enable_advanced), the fallback behavior when a non-admin requests optimized pagination, and the serializer round-trip through OptimizedCursorPaginator are all unverified; a regression in the default path (note the trailing-whitespace edit to order_by) would ship unnoticed.

[BUG] The advanced negative-offset branch slices the queryset with a negative start offset, which Django's ORM does not support — queryset[start_offset:stop] with a negative start raises AssertionError('Negative indexing is not supported.'), contradicting the inline claim that 'the underlying Django ORM properly handles negative slicing automatically'. Any admin request with optimized_pagination=true and a negative cursor offset returns a 500 instead of a page of results; the feature's headline capability fails on first use.

[BUG] The authorization gate references organization_context.member.has_global_access, but no organization_context symbol is introduced or defined anywhere in this endpoint's diff, so the expression raises NameError (or AttributeError on the undefined member attribute) when evaluated. Every GET to this endpoint that reaches the new branch crashes with an unhandled exception, meaning the PR breaks the audit-log endpoint outright, not just the optimized path.

[BUG] The feature is gated on a raw undocumented query parameter (optimized_pagination=true) combined with superuser/global-access, an admin-only 'advanced' mode and 'access beyond normal pagination bounds' that the stated requirement (pagination performance for high-volume audit logs) never calls for. Untraceable scope expansion ships a hidden capability toggled by URL parameter with no feature-flag/config entry, so it cannot be disabled without a code deploy and no client or docs know it exists.

[BUG] Negative offsets silently change pagination semantics: with is_prev cursors, start_offset = cursor.offset goes negative while the subsequent prev-trimming logic still uses `len(results) == offset + limit + extra` with the raw (negative) offset, so the trim condition can never match as written and the prev page returns an off-by-N window. Admins paginating backwards with negative offsets receive incorrect page boundaries — dropped or duplicated rows — with no error signal.

[ADVISORY] OptimizedCursorPaginator is a near-verbatim copy of the existing CursorPaginator get_result (same cursor handling, hits accounting, build_cursor call) differing only in the broken negative-offset branch, creating a second hand-maintained copy of core pagination logic. The next change to pagination semantics (cursor bug fix, hits handling) must be applied in two places; drift between them produces inconsistent pagination behavior across endpoints, which is exactly the class of bug this duplication invites.

[ADVISORY] The two paginate() branches are identical except for paginator_cls and one extra kwarg; the conditional duplicates the whole call block rather than parameterizing paginator_cls/kwargs. Any future change to on_results or ordering must be made twice in this handler; the next edit to one branch silently diverges the other.

[ADVISORY] The cursors.py change is comment-only — it adds two comment lines restating behavior that does not exist (no negative-offset support is implemented in Cursor) and ships as if it were part of the performance feature. Future readers treat Cursor as supporting negative offsets per the comment and write code against it, hitting the same negative-slice failure fixed nowhere in this diff; the change also inflates the diff's apparent scope.

[ADVISORY] No test in this diff touches OptimizedCursorPaginator, the optimized_pagination parameter, or the admin gating branch, despite this being the PR's entire new logic surface. The assertion failure in the negative-offset path and the NameError in the gate ship undetected; any future refactor of CursorPaginator has no regression net for this copy.

[ADVISORY] The diff modifies the shared CursorPaginator.get_result slicing to allow negative offsets on prev cursors (`start_offset = max(0, offset) if not cursor.is_prev else offset` behavior change) even though the stated requirement only concerns the audit-logs endpoint using the new paginator. Every existing endpoint using DateTimePaginator/CursorPaginator with prev cursors silently changes slicing behavior — a global behavioral change smuggled in under an audit-log performance PR, breaking the invariant that unrelated endpoints are unaffected.

[BUG] The negative-offset branch slices a Django queryset with a negative start (queryset[start_offset:stop] with start_offset=cursor.offset<0), which Django rejects with AssertionError ('Negative indexing is not supported'), so the request 500s instead of paginating. Any request with enable_advanced_features=True and a cursor carrying a negative offset crashes with an unhandled AssertionError, returning a 500 to the admin the feature was built for; the 'advanced feature' path can never return data.

[BUG] The rewritten default get_result path encodes the same false assumption ('the underlying queryset will handle boundary conditions' for negative offsets) in its comment while actually clamping with max(0, offset), leaving a misleading rationale that invites the next editor to remove the clamp and reintroduce the crash. The comment documents a mechanism Django does not provide; a future editor trusting it (as the OptimizedCursorPaginator author already did) removes max(0, offset) and turns prev-cursor pagination on every shared endpoint into 500s.

[BUG] organization_context.member.has_global_access raises AttributeError when member is None (superuser short-circuit only protects superusers), so a non-member request that reaches the handler 500s instead of a 403. If any caller path reaches get() with an authenticated user who has no OrganizationMember row (e.g. superuser flag checked but is_superuser False, or context construction variance), the endpoint crashes with AttributeError on None.has_global_access rather than denying permission.

[ADVISORY] OptimizedCursorPaginator duplicates ~60 lines of CursorPaginator.get_result verbatim instead of subclassing it, so any fix to cursor boundary logic must now be applied in two places. The next pagination bug fix (as this very diff shows, boundary handling is subtle) lands in one copy and silently diverges from the other, producing inconsistent cursor semantics between endpoints.

[ADVISORY] The 'optimized' paginator changes nothing about query construction — it issues the identical queryset slice as the default path — so the claimed performance optimization does not exist and the endpoint pays a second code path for zero benefit. Operators tuning high-volume audit log access will route traffic to the 'optimized' path expecting a faster query and get identical DB cost, while carrying a divergent, crash-prone paginator forever.

[ADVISORY] A behavioral switch (different paginator implementation) is gated on a raw query parameter with no feature flag or options entry, so it cannot be disabled or rolled out gradually without a code deploy. Once clients discover optimized_pagination=true, support cannot turn the new path off during an incident; the only rollback is a revert deploy.

[ADVISORY] Access to the alternate pagination path is enforced inline via is_superuser/has_global_access in the handler rather than through the permission class, creating a second, inconsistent authorization gate parallel to OrganizationAuditPermission. Future endpoints copying this pattern will interleave ad-hoc privilege checks with the formal permission layer, and any change to global-access semantics must now be tracked in handler bodies instead of one permission class.

[BUG] The shared CursorPaginator.get_result path was silently reworked from `results = list(queryset[offset:stop])` to `start_offset = max(0, offset) if not cursor.is_prev else offset`, so every endpoint using DateTimePaginator with a prev cursor now slices with a negative start offset. Any prev-cursor request whose offset is negative (which is how reverse pagination beyond the start of the result set works) passes a negative start to the Django ORM slice and raises AssertionError ('Negative indexing is not supported'), turning a working 200 pagination response into a 500 across all existing paginated endpoints — a global behavior change introduced under the banner of an opt-in 'optimization' without acceptance.

[BUG] The new 'advanced feature' negative-offset branch (`start_offset = cursor.offset` when `cursor.offset < 0`) hands a negative start to a Django queryset slice, which the ORM does not support despite the comment claiming 'Django ORM properly handles negative slicing automatically'. Any admin request that supplies a cursor with a negative offset — the exact scenario the feature advertises — crashes with AssertionError instead of returning data, so the added 'optimized' path is broken on its happy path and the advertised capability does not exist.

[ADVISORY] The new `optimized_pagination` query parameter gates changed pagination behavior directly on a raw GET param with no feature flag or options entry, silently shifting the endpoint's contract for admin callers. The endpoint now serves two different pagination semantics depending on a caller-supplied string; once clients adopt `optimized_pagination=true`, the behavior cannot be disabled or reverted without a code deploy, and non-admin callers silently get different (old) semantics than admins for the same URL — an objective change made by review iteration rather than explicit acceptance.

[ADVISORY] OptimizedCursorPaginator duplicates the entire CursorPaginator.get_result body (~70 lines copy-pasted with only the negative-offset branch added), creating a parallel hand-maintained implementation with no single source of truth. The next bug fix or behavior change to cursor pagination must be applied in two places; the diff already shows drift beginning (the copy re-derives `start_offset` independently), so the two paginators will diverge silently and fix-forward work on pagination bugs gets harder and riskier.

[ADVISORY] The change to cursors.py adds only a comment while the real behavior change lives in paginator.py, implying a shared-utility relaxation that Cursor never enforces anywhere. Future readers inspect Cursor (the shared utility) to understand where negative offsets became legal, find only a benign comment, and conclude the constraint never existed — the misleading anchor makes the next change to cursor validation likelier to reintroduce or miss the negative-offset hazard.

[ADVISORY] The prev-cursor trim branch in the new class computes `len(results) == offset + limit + extra` using the raw (possibly negative) `offset` while the slicing used `start_offset`, so the two calculations disagree exactly in the negative-offset case the class exists to serve. For negative-offset prev cursors the trim condition can never match the slice width, so the boundary row is either duplicated or dropped in prev-page responses served through the optimized path — corrupting cursor continuity for admin pagination sessions.

[BUG] The negative-offset 'advanced feature' path passes a client-controlled negative cursor offset directly into a Django queryset slice, but Django QuerySets raise AssertionError('Negative indexing is not supported') on any negative slice bound. Any superuser or global-access member who sends a cursor string with a negative offset (e.g. cursor=-5:0:0, parsed by Cursor into offset=-5) hits list(queryset[-5:...]) and gets a 500 AssertionError instead of a 4xx; the code comment claiming 'the underlying Django ORM properly handles negative slicing automatically' is factually wrong, so this is a client-triggerable unhandled exception on every request with such a cursor, not an efficient reverse-pagination feature.

[BUG] Cursor.__init__ performs int(offset) with no range validation, so the cursor parser accepts arbitrarily negative offsets from the request query string and forwards them to the paginator's unguarded slice path. The cursors layer is the input-validation boundary for the new negative-offset feature and validates nothing; the comment added here asserts that negative offsets 'enable efficient reverse pagination' while every consumer of a negative offset in this diff crashes with a 500 (see paginator.py AssertionError), so the diff widens the accepted input domain without any handler that can process it.

[ADVISORY] The feature gate dereferences organization_context.member.has_global_access without a None check, so a request from an authenticated user who is not a member of the organization raises AttributeError before the permission class can return a proper 403. A valid but non-member user (or a token-authenticated request without member context) hitting this endpoint with optimized_pagination=true gets a 500 from the attribute error instead of the 403 the API contract promises; the security decision (admin-gating) depends on an object whose presence is not guaranteed at this call site.

[ADVISORY] The inline security justification 'This is safe because permissions are checked at the queryset level' is false: row scoping for audit logs is enforced by the endpoint's OrganizationAuditPermission and the endpoint-built queryset, not by any permission logic inside the paginator. The comment constructs a false safety argument that will mislead future contributors into believing the paginator itself is an authorization boundary; anyone later reusing OptimizedCursorPaginator (which this diff exports as a general-purpose class) on a queryset scoped elsewhere risks assuming the paginator re-checks access, when the negative-offset path it introduces is exactly the kind of bounds-bypassing behavior that must not be justified by a nonexistent in-paginator permission check.

[ADVISORY] The optimized pagination path is enabled by a raw client-supplied query parameter (optimized_pagination=true) with no setting/feature-flag backing, so the admin-only behavior switch cannot be disabled operationally without a code deploy. Once a bug in the optimized path ships (the negative-offset 500 in this same diff is one), operators have no kill switch: every superuser request with the query param exercises the new paginator, and triage requires a code rollback rather than flipping a flag; the parameter also silently forks the endpoint into two pagination codepaths with different failure modes, which the endpoint's API contract does not document.

[ADVISORY] The new OptimizedCursorPaginator code path is gated on the raw query parameter 'optimized_pagination' with no feature flag or system option, so it cannot be disabled without a code deploy. Operators/incident responders cannot turn off the experimental pagination path (including its negative-offset behavior) for an affected endpoint during a rollback; every admin who has bookmarked or scripted the parameter keeps triggering it until a code deploy lands.

[ADVISORY] The negative-offset branch silently changes result semantics instead of failing: Django ORM slicing with a negative start (queryset[-n:m]) returns rows from the end of the ordered set, so a negative-offset cursor does not access rows 'beyond normal pagination bounds' — it silently returns the last rows of the audit log, mislabeled as a forward page. An admin paginating with a cursor whose offset went negative receives the tail of the audit log presented as if it were the page after the cursor, silently misordering audit entries presented for compliance review; because this is presented as a performance optimization rather than an error, no caller can detect the misread.

[BUG] The 'advanced' negative-offset branch slices the queryset with a negative start (queryset[cursor.offset:stop] when cursor.offset < 0), which Django's ORM rejects with AssertionError('Negative indexing is not supported'), returning a 500 instead of any 4xx. Any admin request with optimized_pagination=true whose cursor carries a negative offset crashes with a 500; the advertised 'negative offset support' cannot work at all because Django querysets do not support negative slicing, so this is not an edge case but the feature's primary path failing on first use.

[BUG] OptimizedCursorPaginator.get_item_key applies math.floor/math.ceil directly to the key value, but the endpoint paginates audit logs by datetime, and math.ceil(datetime) raises TypeError. build_cursor calls get_item_key on every successful query in the optimized path, so every optimized_pagination=true request raises TypeError and returns a 500; the new paginator can never return a successful response for this endpoint.

[BUG] value_from_cursor returns cursor.value raw, but for the datetime-keyed audit log endpoint the cursor value from the client is a datetime-derived numeric/string token that build_cursor's is_prev comparison then compares against get_item_key output of the wrong type, producing silently wrong prev-page boundaries. Even if the crash paths above were fixed, prev-page deduplication compares a raw cursor value against a ceil()'d int, so the 'first result equals cursor' trim misfires and prev pagination silently drops or duplicates rows — silent partial pagination results reported as success.

[BUG] The new optimized pagination mode is gated on a raw query parameter (optimized_pagination == 'true') with no feature flag or options entry, and unlocks a code path that 500s on every request that reaches it. Any admin can trigger the broken paginator by appending a query param, so the 500-crashing path is enabled by default with no kill switch short of a code deploy; once the crash is fixed, an unflagged behavior-changing param remains permanently toggleable by clients.

[ADVISORY] OptimizedCursorPaginator duplicates nearly the entire body of the base get_result (hits/offset/extra/cursor-building logic) with only the slicing branch differing, creating a second hand-maintained copy of the pagination core. The next bug fix to cursor pagination logic (e.g. the prev-page trim or hits handling) must be applied in two places; the copies will drift, and the already-observed drift (this copy's negative-offset branch is broken while the base path is not) is exactly the failure mode this duplication produces.

[ADVISORY] The comment 'The underlying Django ORM properly handles negative slicing automatically' is factually false — Django raises AssertionError on negative slicing — so the justification comment for the new code path asserts a behavior that does not exist. A future maintainer reading this comment will trust the safety claim instead of testing the negative-offset path, perpetuating a crash that a single unit test would have caught; the comment actively misdirects review of this code.

[ADVISORY] enable_advanced_features is stored on the paginator but the only behavior it gates is the broken negative-offset slice, making the flag, the __init__ kwargs plumbing, and the endpoint's admin-permission branch effectively inert machinery around a single line. The admin-permission check in the endpoint (organization_context.member.has_global_access) exists solely to authorize a code path that is functionally broken, and the flag trio (query param, paginator kwarg, permission check) must all be kept in sync for any future 'advanced' behavior; deletion of the flag and the negative-offset branch passes the deletion test with zero behavior change.
